title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR ALL? BRAZILIAN TEACHERS ON ETHICS, EQUITY, AND THE EVERYDAY CHALLENGES OF AI IN EDUCATION
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how Brazilian K-12 educators perceive artificial intelligence in education, with a particular focus on general-purpose and generative AI, and on issues of ethics, equity, and everyday implementation barriers. The study is motivated by the tension between AI’s potential to improve teaching and personalize learning and Brazil’s persistent structural inequalities in access to digital infrastructure, training, and policy support. The authors ask whether educators believe AI can benefit education, which benefits matter most, whether ethical issues should be taught in schools, whether teachers have sufficient training resources, and what challenges most constrain adoption.

The study uses a nationwide quantitative survey of 346 education professionals in Brazil, primarily teachers but also school managers and other school staff. A 35-item questionnaire, grounded in Brazil’s Framework of Teachers’ Digital Competencies, was distributed online via Google Forms between October 28, 2024 and February 28, 2025. Items addressed three broad areas: teaching and learning with digital technologies, digital citizenship, and professional development. The survey examined participants’ AI literacy, perceived educational uses of AI, views on ethics instruction, and perceived barriers such as training, technical support, time, and infrastructure.

Participants worked across Brazilian K-12 contexts, including early primary, upper primary, and secondary education, with representation from all regions of Brazil and from public and private schools, mostly urban. Results showed that most respondents had only basic or limited knowledge of AI, yet were strongly interested in using it. The most frequently perceived benefits were creating interactive content, lesson planning, personalized assessment, inclusion, and identifying students’ learning difficulties. Teachers also saw value in AI for reducing workload, supporting data-informed teaching, and helping with continuous professional development. At the same time, they emphasized the need to discuss ethics, digital citizenship, bias, transparency, and technological dependence with students.

The paper concludes that Brazilian educators are receptive to AI but that effective and equitable implementation is constrained by insufficient teacher training, lack of technical support, inadequate infrastructure, and the absence of a national top-down curriculum or implementation framework. The authors characterize Brazil as still operating under a bottom-up model of AI integration. They recommend free online continuous professional development, curricular integration of ethics and digital citizenship, and stronger public investment in infrastructure and support so that AI adoption in Brazilian K-12 education can be ethical, inclusive, and context-sensitive.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: General-purpose artificial intelligence, including generative AI systems, discussed as a broad category rather than a specific product.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied via a nationwide questionnaire of Brazilian K-12 educators about their literacy, perceived benefits, ethical concerns, training needs, and implementation challenges related to using AI/GenAI in education.

findings.finding_summary: Among 346 Brazilian educators, 97.3% identified at least one positive educational use of AI. The most frequently cited operational uses were creation of interactive content (80.6%), lesson planning (80.2%), researching relevant content (80.6%), creating assessments and exercises (70.9%), curation of digital content (66.3%), and remixing/adapting materials (51.2%), indicating strong perceived potential for workload reduction and teaching support.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported perceptions of AI benefits for teaching support and workload optimization from questionnaire responses

findings.finding_summary: Educators reported strong perceived benefits of AI for personalization and inclusion. Specifically, 68.6% selected personalized assessment, 65.5% selected inclusion potential, 47.7% selected identification of students’ learning difficulties, 79.8% highlighted identifying learning trends, 71.3% highlighted personalized learning strategies, 70.9% highlighted integration of assistive technologies, 60.5% collaborative learning environments, and 53.5% monitoring student progress; only 0.8% said they did not believe AI could promote inclusion.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported perceptions of AI for personalized learning, inclusive practice, and student support

findings.finding_summary: The survey found strong educator interest but major implementation barriers. While 97.3% showed interest in AI’s potential and more than 80% expressed interest in AI professional development, 80.3% had only basic or limited AI knowledge; 50.8% had not taken any AI course but were interested, and key barriers were lack of training (43.4%), reliable equipment/internet (43.0%), lack of technical support (41.9%), and time to learn new tools (34.5%).
findings.measure: Teacher-reported AI literacy, training participation, institutional support, and implementation barriers

findings.finding_summary: Teachers strongly endorsed AI-related digital citizenship and ethics education for students. In the sample, 78.3% considered it essential to address ethical issues related to AI, 73.6% emphasized teaching students to critically evaluate AI-generated information, 70.2% highlighted reflection on technological dependence, 64.3% stressed teacher training in ethics and safety, and 61.2% emphasized transparency and bias mitigation.
findings.measure: Teacher-reported importance of AI ethics, critical evaluation, and responsible use in student education

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical nationwide survey of educator perceptions with a clearly described questionnaire and sample, but it does not evaluate causal effects of an intervention on student outcomes. Evidence is based on self-reported perceptions rather than experimental or quasi-experimental impact estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports strong positive perceptions and substantial implementation challenges, but no direct effect sizes or measured student learning impacts. Overall impact is therefore promising but unclear.
